synopsis: For brake-commanding heavy off-road functions, the corpus uses ISO 19014 Machine Performance Levels rather than ISO 26262/ASIL; MPL uses levels a–e and is tailored to earth-moving machinery [f2071, f12035, f12066]. Hazard analysis through the Part 1 Machine Control System Safety Analysis (MCSSA) assigns MPLr, and design evaluation must demonstrate MPLa at least as high, with Part 2 addressing architecture, reliability and fault behavior [f15169, f2337]. Part 5 tables can replace a full MCSSA for each new model when their use-case assumptions hold, but the booklet neither reviewed a collision-avoidance/automatic-braking table entry nor found a published MPLr for that function [f2332, f2334, f2335]. The standards baseline needs confirmation: Chapter 8 marks its Part 5 evidence as draft, while other passages describe normative tables and report second editions of Parts 1–4 and the first full edition of Part 5 under publication for October 2026 [f6284, f10523, f12041]. The planning recommendation is an approved MCSSA before prototype arrival, covering failure to intervene and incorrect intervention, allocated performance levels and requirements-to-test traceability; postponing these decisions risks consuming the four-month validation window in debate rather than evidence gathering [f10530, f10540]. MPLr determines the redundancy, diagnostics and evidence needed for the braking chain, and the functional safety engineer expects both required and achieved levels to be allocated [f12046, f11088].
